section.heading: Solve Radical Equations
section.paragraph: In this section we will solve equations that have a variable in the radicand of a radical expression. An equation of this type is called a radical equation.

note.title: Radical Equation
note.paragraph: An equation in which a variable is in the radicand of a radical expression is called a radical equation.

section.paragraph: As usual, when solving these equations, what we do to one side of an equation we must do to the other side as well. Once we isolate the radical, our strategy will be to raise both sides of the equation to the power of the index. This will eliminate the radical.

Solving radical equations containing an even index by raising both sides to the power of the index may introduce an algebraic solution that would not be a solution to the original radical equation. Again, we call this an extraneous solution as we did when we solved rational equations.
In the next example, we will see how to solve a radical equation. Our strategy is based on raising a radical with index n to the nth power. This will eliminate the radical.
$$\text{For} a \geq 0, \left( \sqrt[n]{a} \right)^{n} = a.$$

example.title: How to Solve a Radical Equation

note.title: How To
note.heading: Solve a radical equation with one radical.

list.item: Step 1. Isolate the radical on one side of the equation.
Step 2. Raise both sides of the equation to the power of the index.
Step 3. Solve the new equation.
Step 4. Check the answer in the original equation.

section.paragraph: When we use a radical sign, it indicates the principal or positive root. If an equation has a radical with an even index equal to a negative number, that equation will have no solution.

row.cell: To isolate the radical, subtract 1 to both sides.

solution.paragraph: Because the square root is equal to a negative number, the equation has no solution.

section.paragraph: If one side of an equation with a square root is a binomial, we use the Product of Binomial Squares Pattern when we square it.

note.title: Binomial Squares
note.paragraph: $$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ {\left( {a + b} \right)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}} \\ {\left( {a - b} \right)^{2} = a^{2} - 2ab + b^{2}} \end{matrix}$$

section.paragraph: Don’t forget the middle term!

row.cell: To isolate the radical, subtract 1 from both sides.
Square both sides of the equation.
Simplify, using the Product of Binomial Squares Pattern on theright. Then solve the new equation.
It is a quadratic equation, so get zero on one side.

section.paragraph: When the index of the radical is 3, we cube both sides to remove the radical.
$$\left( \sqrt[3]{a} \right)^{3} = a$$

row.cell: To isolate the radical, subtract 8 from both sides.
Cube both sides of the equation.

section.paragraph: Sometimes an equation will contain rational exponents instead of a radical. We use the same techniques to solve the equation as when we have a radical. We raise each side of the equation to the power of the denominator of the rational exponent. Since $$\left( a^{m} \right)^{n} = a^{m \cdot n},$$ we have for example,
$$\left( x^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2} = x,\left( x^{\frac{1}{3}} \right)^{3} = x$$
Remember, $$x^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{x}$$ and $$x^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{x}.$$

row.cell: To isolate the term with the rational exponent,subtract 3 from both sides.
Raise each side of the equation to the fourth power.

section.paragraph: Sometimes the solution of a radical equation results in two algebraic solutions, but one of them may be an extraneous solution!

row.cell: Square both sides of the equation.
Simplify and then solve the equation
It is a quadratic equation, so get zero onone side.

section.paragraph: When there is a coefficient in front of the radical, we must raise it to the power of the index, too.

row.cell: Isolate the radical by dividing both sides by 3.
Square both sides of the equation.
Simplify, then solve the new equation.

section.heading: Solve Radical Equations with Two Radicals
section.paragraph: If the radical equation has two radicals, we start out by isolating one of them. It often works out easiest to isolate the more complicated radical first.

section.paragraph: Sometimes after raising both sides of an equation to a power, we still have a variable inside a radical. When that happens, we repeat Step 1 and Step 2 of our procedure. We isolate the radical and raise both sides of the equation to the power of the index again.

example.title: How to Solve a Radical Equation

section.paragraph: We summarize the steps here. We have adjusted our previous steps to include more than one radical in the equation This procedure will now work for any radical equations.

list.item: Step 1. Isolate one of the radical terms on one side of the equation.
Step 2. Raise both sides of the equation to the power of the index.
Step 3. Are there any more radicals? If yes, repeat Step 1 and Step 2 again. If no, solve the new equation.
Step 4. Check the answer in the original equation.

section.heading: Use Radicals in Applications
section.paragraph: As you progress through your college courses, you’ll encounter formulas that include radicals in many disciplines. We will modify our Problem Solving Strategy for Geometry Applications slightly to give us a plan for solving applications with formulas from any discipline.

note.title: How To
note.heading: Use a problem solving strategy for applications with formulas.

list.item: Step 1. Read the problem and make sure all the words and ideas are understood. When appropriate, draw a figure and label it with the given information.
Step 2. Identify what we are looking for.
Step 3. Name what we are looking for by choosing a variable to represent it.
Step 4. Translate into an equation by writing the appropriate formula or model for the situation. Substitute in the given information.
Step 5. Solve the equation using good algebra techniques.
Step 6. Check the answer in the problem and make sure it makes sense.
Step 7. Answer the question with a complete sentence.

section.paragraph: One application of radicals has to do with the effect of gravity on falling objects. The formula allows us to determine how long it will take a fallen object to hit the gound.

note.title: Falling Objects
note.paragraph: On Earth, if an object is dropped from a height of h feet, the time in seconds it will take to reach the ground is found by using the formula

section.paragraph: For example, if an object is dropped from a height of 64 feet, we can find the time it takes to reach the ground by substituting $$h = 64$$ into the formula.
It would take 2 seconds for an object dropped from a height of 64 feet to reach the ground.

problem.paragraph: Marissa dropped her sunglasses from a bridge 400 feet above a river. Use the formula $$t = \frac{\sqrt{h}}{4}$$ to find how many seconds it took for the sunglasses to reach the river.
